title: Darwin, Northern Territory
description: Capital city of Northern Territory, Australia
wiki_lead:
Darwin (  DAR-win; Larrakia: Garramilla) is the capital and largest city of the Northern Territory, Australia. The city had a population of 139,902 at the 2021 census, which is nearly 63% of the territory's population. It is the smallest, wettest, and most northerly of the Australian capital cities and serves as the Top End's regional centre.
Darwin's proximity to Southeast Asia makes it a key link between Australia and countries such as Indonesia and Timor-Leste. The Stuart Highway begins in Darwin and extends southwards across central Australia through Tennant Creek and Alice Springs, concluding in Port Augusta, South Australia. The city is built upon a low bluff overlooking Darwin Harbour. Darwin's suburbs extend to Lee Point in the north and to Berrimah in the east. The Stuart Highway extends to Darwin's eastern satellite city of Palmerston and its suburbs.
The Darwin region, like much of the Top End, has a tropical climate, with a wet and dry season. A period known locally as "the build up" leading up to Darwin's wet season sees temperature and humidity increase. Darwin's wet season typically arrives in late November to early December and brings with it heavy monsoonal downpours, spectacular lightning displays, and increased cyclone activity. During the dry season, the city has clear skies and mild sea breezes from the harbour.
The Larrakia people are the traditional owners of the Darwin area, and Aboriginal people are a significant proportion of the population. On 9 September 1839, HMS Beagle sailed into Darwin Harbour during its survey of the area. John Clements Wickham named the region "Port Darwin" in honour of Charles Darwin, who had sailed with them on the ship's previous voyage. The settlement there became the town of Palmerston in 1869, but was renamed Darwin in 1911. Darwin has been almost entirely rebuilt four times, following devastation caused by a cyclone in 1897, another one in 1937, Japanese air raids during World War II, and Cyclone Tracy in 1974.

History


Indigenous history
The Aboriginal people of the Larrakia language group are the traditional custodians and earliest known inhabitants of the greater Darwin area. Their name for the area is Garramilla, pronounced  and meaning "white stone", referring to the colour of rock and sea cliffs found in the area. They had trading routes with Southeast Asia (see Macassan contact with Australia) and imported goods from as far afield as South and Western Australia. Established songlines penetrated throughout the country, allowing stories and histories to be told and retold along the routes.


Pre-20th century

The Dutch visited Australia's northern coastline in the 1600s and landed on the Tiwi Islands only to be attacked by the Tiwi peoples. The Dutch created the first European maps of the area. This accounts for the Dutch names in the area, such as Arnhem Land and Groote Eylandt. During this period, Dutch explorers named the region around Darwin—sometimes including nearby Kimberley
grok_lead: Darwin is the capital city of Australia's Northern Territory, located on the northern coastline adjacent to the Timor Sea in the Top End region. Founded in 1869 as Palmerston to serve as a settlement and port, it was renamed Darwin in 1911 in honor of the naturalist Charles Darwin, reflecting its strategic role in European exploration and administration of the continent's north. The Greater Darwin area had an estimated resident population of 152,489 as of June 2024, comprising over half of the territory's total residents and featuring a diverse demographic with significant Indigenous Australian representation. The city experiences a tropical savanna climate with distinct wet (November to April) and dry seasons, marked by high humidity, monsoonal rainfall averaging over 1,700 mm annually, and average temperatures ranging from 24â32Â°C year-round, occasionally disrupted by cyclones. As the territory's primary administrative, commercial, and export hub, Darwin's economy relies on public sector activities, defence installations, mining and liquefied natural gas exports via its deep-water port, tourism drawn to its proximity to natural attractions, and construction tied to resource projects. Key historical events defining its resilience include the 1942 Japanese air raids during World War II, which targeted its military and port facilities, and Cyclone Tracy in 1974, which demolished 80% of the urban structures and necessitated a complete modern reconstruction emphasizing cyclone-resistant design.
